claims.label: Individual differences supply the material for natural selection
claims.statement: The slight individual differences among members of a species provide the materials that natural selection accumulates, in the same way that man accumulates individual differences in domestic productions.

operationalizations.text: Test whether standing within-population additive genetic variance (V_A or G-matrix) and standing genetic polymorphism in wild populations predict the direction and rate of adaptive divergence across populations and closely related species.

Measure heritable within-species differences and test whether selection differentials on them predict allele-frequency or trait shifts across generations. Repeatable directional accumulation supports the mechanism; absence of heritable variation or response refutes it.

Estimate heritability of ordinary within-species individual differences and the response to selection on those differences, as opposed to responses that require rare sports or new mutations. Positive heritability and a response attributable to standing individual differences would support the claim; evolution that proceeds only by rare macromutations, or individual differences that are never heritable, would refute it.

obstacles: Over long macroevolutionary timescales, new mutations rather than initial standing individual differences increasingly contribute to divergence.
Field selection estimates can be environmentally confounded.
Well-studied taxa are nonrandom.
Sequence differences are a reinterpretation of the visible individual differences Darwin treated as the raw material.
Heritability and selection response are scattered across studies and are not columns in the barcode archives.
The statement is close to the definition of selection on standing variation once heritability is granted.

claims.label: Larger genera tend to grow larger and dominant forms more dominant
claims.statement: Because the dominant species of larger genera vary most and varieties become new species, larger genera tend to become larger, and dominant forms tend to become more dominant by leaving many modified, dominant descendants.

operationalizations.text: Test in the fossil record and dated phylogenies whether species richness and geographic occupancy/abundance at time t positively predict net diversification rate and daughter clade dominance at time t+1, versus diversity-dependent slowdown or peak-and-decline dynamics.

Using fossil and dated phylogenetic time slices, test whether initially species-rich genera have higher subsequent net diversification and whether widespread abundant lineages leave more dominant descendants. Positive temporal effects support the prediction.

Test whether larger genera tend to gain species through time more than smaller ones, and whether species that are widespread and abundant leave more descendant species that are themselves widespread. A positive richness trend and a positive descendant-dominance relationship, above a passive-diffusion null, would support the prediction; large genera shrinking as often as they grow, or dominant species leaving no more dominant descendants, would count against it.

obstacles: Ecological saturation and mass extinctions periodically overturn dominant clades (as Darwin himself noted in ch02-09), creating a tension between short-term preferential growth and long-term clade turnover.
Survivorship bias can create apparent rich-get-richer patterns.
Dominance has no single cross-taxon measure.
Large genera are expected to wander more under a passive null, so growth is not automatically a driven trend.
Abundance and dominance of ancestors are barely preserved, so descendant dominance is proxied by living range.
Extant trees lack the failed lineages that would have made dominant groups look less inevitably successful.

claims.label: Where many species of a genus have formed, many are still forming
claims.statement: On the view that species are strongly marked varieties, where many species of a genus have been formed, on average many new species should still be forming.

operationalizations.text: Correlate total genus species richness (or recent diversification rate over the past few million years) with current tip-level speciation rate estimates (e.g., DR statistic, BAMM/ClaDS tip rates) or count of incipient species/subspecies across large dated phylogenies.

Estimate current incipient-speciation rates from genomic divergence, reproductive isolation and lineage splitting, then test whether they increase with existing genus richness after age and sampling controls. A positive average relationship supports the prediction.

Compare recent speciation rates, or counts of subspecies and phylogeographic splits, with present genus richness. A positive average relationship would support the prediction that where many species have formed, many are still forming; no relationship, or a negative one, would refute it.

obstacles: Diversity-dependent slowdowns in old saturated clades can cause some very large genera to have declining current speciation rates compared to young radiating genera.
'Still forming' is not directly observable.
Genus age and taxonomic practice strongly confound richness.
Tip-rate estimators are biased by tree shape, sampling fraction, and taxonomic splitting.
Subspecies counts repeat the effort bias that affects variety counts.
A large genus can be old and slow, which satisfies 'many have formed' without 'many are still forming'.

claims.label: Males of polygamous species fight most and carry special weapons
claims.statement: Fighting between males for females is perhaps most severe in polygamous animals, and the males of such species are the most often equipped with special weapons.

operationalizations.text: Perform phylogenetic comparative analyses across animal clades (e.g. mammals, birds, beetles) testing whether polygynous mating systems significantly predict the presence and relative size of male weaponry (antlers, horns, spurs, enlarged mandibles) and intensity of male-male combat.

Across a phylogenetically controlled sample, regress observed male combat intensity and weapon presence or size on mating-system polygyny. Higher combat and weapon prevalence in polygynous species support the claim; no association or stronger effects in monogamous species refute it.

Code mating system, male-combat frequency, and presence of weapons, then fit a phylogenetic regression. The claim would be confirmed if polygynous lineages have higher combat rates and weapon frequencies than monogamous relatives after body size and habitat are controlled; it would be refuted if weapon evolution is independent of mating system. Combat itself is usually proxied by weaponry and sexual size dimorphism.

obstacles: Categorical classifications of social mating systems (monogamous vs polygamous) can mask genetic extra-pair paternity and continuous variation in the opportunity for sexual selection.
Some weapons also function in anti-predator defence, requiring control for female weapon presence and predation regime.
Combat intensity and 'special weapons' require subjective coding.
Trait databases have substantial missingness and study bias.
Mating system and weapon inventories are spread through handbooks and supplements rather than one global table.
Weapons proxy fighting and can also function in display or predator defence.
Birds are less consistently coded than large mammals.

claims.label: Natural selection works only by accumulating very small modifications
claims.statement: Natural selection acts only by preserving and accumulating very small inherited modifications, each profitable to its bearer, and so excludes continued creation of new organisms or large sudden changes of structure.

operationalizations.text: Examine the distribution of phenotypic effect sizes of adaptive Quantitative Trait Loci (QTLs), beneficial mutations, and chromosomal/structural variants (including polyploidy and major-effect loci) underlying adaptive divergence; the strict claim that selection acts *only* on infinitesimally small modifications is refuted if large-effect mutations or saltational changes (e.g. whole-genome duplications, major-effect loci) regularly contribute to adaptation.

For documented adaptive transitions, estimate effect sizes of causal inherited variants and reconstruct whether phenotypic change accumulated through small beneficial steps or large-effect mutations. Recurrent adaptive large-effect changes would refute the exclusive 'infinitesimally small' assertion.

Compile the effect sizes of alleles that have contributed to retained adaptive change, and the frequency of polyploid and other macromutational origins. The strict reading would be confirmed only if preserved adaptations are overwhelmingly built from tiny-effect steps. It would be refuted if large-effect alleles or whole-genome duplications repeatedly constitute the inherited change that is kept.

obstacles: The Beavis effect (upward bias in estimated QTL effect sizes in small mapping populations) can inflate apparent effect sizes of detected loci.
What counts as 'infinitesimally small' versus 'large sudden change' lies along a continuum, though extreme cases (whole-genome duplication, major homeotic/supergene shifts) are clear.
The phrase 'infinitesimally small' lacks a unique modern threshold.
Surviving genomic signatures underrepresent old or polygenic adaptations.
Infinitesimally small can be read as a population-genetic limit or as a ban on large mutations, and those readings diverge.
GWAS and QTL samples are biased toward large effects and toward crops, livestock, and humans.
A large-effect allele can still be followed by a long series of small modifiers.

claims.label: Freshwater biotas evolve and go extinct more slowly, keeping relict forms
claims.statement: Because all freshwater basins together form a small area, competition among freshwater organisms has been less severe, so new forms have arisen more slowly and old forms have been exterminated more slowly there, which is why fresh water holds ancient and anomalous forms.

operationalizations.text: Compare speciation rates, extinction rates, mean lineage age, and morphological evolutionary rates among freshwater, marine, and terrestrial clades using time-calibrated molecular phylogenies and the fossil record.

Compare freshwater, marine and terrestrial lineages for origination, extinction, lineage age and phylogenetic distinctiveness. Slower turnover and a greater excess of old isolated lineages in freshwater support the prediction, although competition would require separate evidence.

Compare speciation and extinction rates, and the stem ages of living species-poor lineages, among freshwater, marine, and terrestrial clades. Lower origination and extinction in fresh water, plus an excess of old relict lineages, would confirm the claim; equal or higher freshwater rates in well-preserved groups would refute it.

obstacles: Freshwater habitats are highly fragmented into isolated river basins and lakes rather than acting as a single small basin, which actually drives rapid allopatric speciation in many teleost groups (e.g. cichlids, ostariophysans) contrary to Darwin's premise.
Taphonomic preservation rates in freshwater sediments differ substantially from marine shelf environments.
Freshwater fossil preservation and sampling differ from marine records.
Turnover differences cannot by themselves identify competition as the cause.
Freshwater fossils are preserved less completely than marine shelly faunas.
Relict is a judgment about morphological oddity as well as phylogenetic age.
Habitat shifts move lineages across the categories being compared.

claims.label: Each species arose in a single area and spread from there
claims.statement: Each species was first produced in one area only and subsequently migrated from that area as far as its powers of migration and subsistence allowed under past and present conditions, rather than arising independently at several points.

operationalizations.text: Test whether conspecific populations across a species' geographic range form a monophyletic lineage tracing to a single geographic origin in phylogeographic reconstructions, rather than arising polyphyletically from distinct local ancestors in separate regions.

For species with dense genomic and occurrence sampling, infer ancestral geographic origin and expansion history and test monophyly of populations against independent polycentric origins. Repeated well-supported single origins would support the generalization.

For species with range-wide genetic sampling, ask whether gene trees fit one ancestral area followed by spread, or require two or more unrelated origins. A substantial share of species with well-supported multiple origins would challenge the claim.

obstacles: Recurrent polyploid speciation in plants and rare parallel ecological speciation can produce polyphyletic origins of the same nominal species or ecomorph in multiple localities.
Species boundaries and geographic origins are often uncertain.
Extinction erases source populations.
A single-origin model can be difficult to distinguish from gene flow after multiple origins.
Range-wide sequences exist for a small fraction of species.
Cryptic species and over-lumped names can look like multiple origins of one species.
Published phylogeographies would have to be compiled, which is months of work at global scope.

claims.label: Homologous parts tend to vary together
claims.statement: Parts of the body that are homologous and alike early in embryonic development, such as left and right sides or fore and hind limbs, tend to vary in a correlated way.

operationalizations.text: Compute phenotypic ($\mathbf{P}$) and additive genetic ($\mathbf{G}$) correlation matrices across bilateral structures (left vs right side) and serially homologous structures (forelimb vs hindlimb elements, serial vertebrae, floral whorls) and test whether homologous pairs exhibit significantly higher correlation than non-homologous trait pairs.

Estimate within-individual and genetic covariance in size, shape or developmental perturbation among homologous bilateral or serial parts. Positive covariance exceeding that among nonhomologous matched parts supports the claim; independence or negative covariance refutes it.

Within species, correlate measurements of serial and bilateral homologs and compare those correlations with correlations between non-homologous parts. Stronger covariation among homologs would confirm the claim; correlations indistinguishable from non-homologous pairs would refute it. Genetic correlations in model organisms are a second, mechanistic layer.

obstacles: Functional divergence (e.g. bats, bipedal mammals, birds) can actively select for reduced integration (parcellation) between forelimbs and hindlimbs relative to quadrupedal ancestors.
Public morphology repositories often lack pedigrees needed for genetic covariance.
Shared mechanical use can correlate homologues without shared developmental variation.
Within-species covariance matrices are published piecemeal, not as a global download.
AVONET does not pair forelimb and hindlimb homologs across animals generally.
Measuring existing scans at comparative scale is months of work.

claims.label: Congeners differ more in secondary sexual characters than in other parts
claims.statement: Secondary sexual characters are highly variable, and species of the same group differ from one another more in their secondary sexual characters than in other parts of their organisation.

operationalizations.text: Compare both intraspecific coefficients of variation (CV) and interspecific evolutionary divergence rates ($\sigma^2$) between secondary sexual characters (male ornaments, weapons, courtship signals) and non-sexual somatic traits across congeneric animal species.

Within genera or families, compare standardized among-species divergence and within-species variance for secondary sexual traits versus other morphology. Larger values for sexual traits support the claim; comparable or smaller divergence refutes it.

Within clades, compare evolutionary disparity in secondary sexual traits with disparity in other measured structures, using sex-specific data. Greater disparity in the sexual traits would confirm the claim; equal or greater disparity in non-sexual traits would refute it.

obstacles: Allometric scaling of large ornaments with body size can inflate raw variance if not residualized against body size.
Trait classes need comparable scaling and sampling.
Public media and specimens are heavily biased toward birds and conspicuous traits.
Global morphology tables are mostly unsexed and omit plumage and other ornaments.
Showy characters receive more taxonomic attention, which inflates their apparent disparity.
Sex-specific compilations are dense for a few groups, such as galliforms and lizards, and sparse elsewhere.

claims.label: The bond linking inhabitants of the same area through space and time is inheritance
claims.statement: The deep affinity uniting the living and extinct inhabitants of the same area, independent of physical conditions, is due to inheritance from common ancestors, while the differences among regions arise mainly from modification through natural selection and only subordinately from the direct influence of physical conditions.

operationalizations.text: Test for spatial phylogenetic clustering (monophyly and patristic proximity of regional living and fossil taxa) and compare models of trait evolution driven by biotic diversification versus direct abiotic correlation across biogeographic realms.

Test whether regional living and fossil assemblages share phylogenetic ancestry beyond environmental matching, then partition trait and lineage turnover among inherited regional history, selection-associated environment, and direct plastic responses. Support requires strong geographic phylogenetic continuity not explained by physical conditions.

Ask whether regional biotas form phylogenetic clusters on molecular trees built independently of the morphological resemblance naturalists scored, and whether regional trait differences exceed what the physical environment predicts. Shared ancestry can be assessed that way; attributing the differences mainly to natural selection remains weakly separated from other causes.

obstacles: Phylogenetic trees built under evolutionary models assume common descent, so testing common ancestry requires evaluating tree-like signal (hierarchical character congruence) across independent genomic and morphological loci.
Separating natural selection driven by biotic interactions from selection driven by physical conditions is difficult in macroevolutionary datasets.
Inheritance, selection, and direct environmental effects are not cleanly separable observationally.
Fossil and living taxonomies are unevenly linked.
A tree built from the same traits that display the affinity would make the inheritance test circular.
Selection, drift, and direct effects of the environment are not separated by present distributions.
Joint phylogenetic and geographic coverage is partial for the full living and fossil scope.
